query: For high-entropy-alloy materials intended for self-lubricating moving components, what single intervention could reduce both coefficient of friction and wear rate across a wide service-temperature range? Formulate one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts the improvement relative to the untreated alloy, defines the conditions under which it should remain effective, cites prior evidence supporting it, and proposes an experiment whose outcome could falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Laser surface cladding a high-entropy alloy (HEA) with a controlled amount of tungsten carbide (WC) nanoparticle reinforcement will induce dynamic, self-adaptive, nano‐structured tribolayers during sliding that lower both the coefficient of friction and wear rate over a broad temperature range.
generation.material_initial_state: An untreated single‐phase or multi‐phase HEA used in self‐lubricating moving components that displays typical friction and wear behavior under operational conditions.
generation.intervention: Apply a laser cladding process to deposit a thin surface layer of the HEA with a small, optimized WC nanoparticle content (e.g., ~0.2 mass % WC) on the sliding interface.
generation.conditions: Tested across a wide service-temperature range, from room temperature to at least 800 °C, and under typical sliding/contact loads encountered in moving components.
generation.structural_mediator: The incorporation and partial decomposition of WC leads to lattice distortion and grain refinement in the cladding layer, resulting in a nanohierarchical architecture with coexisting ultra-fine grains and dispersed nanoprecipitates. This structure promotes the formation of a self-organized, adaptive tribolayer (or nano-glaze) during sliding.
generation.mechanism: During operation, the refined surface microstructure mediates a multi-type adaptive friction interface protection. WC-derived species and the engineered nanostructure facilitate the in situ formation of a lubricious glaze layer (or ultra-nanocrystalline near-surface layer) that both reduces friction by acting as a barrier to dislocation motion and minimizes wear by distributing contact stresses over a larger area.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the untreated HEA, the intervention is expected to reduce the coefficient of friction by roughly 25–30% and decrease the wear rate by at least a factor of 2, while maintaining these improvements over the entire service-temperature range.
generation.baseline: The untreated HEA displays higher friction (e.g., COF around 0.3 or greater in some controlled environments) and wear rates (e.g., on the order of 10^(-6) mm3/N-m or similar values reported in literature) when tested under similar conditions.
generation.boundary: The beneficial effects of the surface modification are anticipated as long as the cladding layer remains intact and the nanohierarchical structure is preserved during operation; excessive temperature spikes, aggressive corrosive environments, or mechanical impacts that disrupt the cladded layer could negate the improvements.
generation.uncertainty: The precise quantitative improvements may vary with the exact WC content, processing parameters, and operating conditions. Additionally, the long-term stability and regeneration capacity of the self-adaptive tribolayer under cyclic or extreme loading still require verification.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of high-entropy alloy samples: one set with the laser-cladded WC nanoparticle-reinforced surface layer and another set as the untreated control. Subject both sets to identical reciprocating sliding wear tests over a temperature range from room temperature to 800 °C. Monitor the evolution of the surface microstructure using TEM/SEM and record tribological parameters (friction coefficient and wear rate) in real time.
measurements: Coefficient of friction using a tribometer across varying temperatures
Wear volume loss measured by profilometry
Surface morphology and nanostructure analysis via SEM/TEM before and after tests
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the cladded samples do not exhibit a statistically significant reduction (e.g., less than ~25% reduction in COF and less than 50% decrease in wear rate) compared to the untreated control across the tested temperature range, or if no evidence of a self-adaptive tribolayer formation is observed, then the hypothesis is falsified.

Remarkable Wear Resistance in a Complex Concentrated Alloy with Nanohierarchical Architecture and Composition Undulation

Abstract: AbstractSustained wear damages on the sliding surfaces of alloys are generally the culprit responsible for the failure of various mechanical systems. Inspired by high-entropy effects, here we deliberately deploy nanohierarchical architecture with composition undulation in a Ni50(AlNbTiV)50 complex concentrated alloy, which yields ultralow wear rate within the order of 10−7 to 10−6 mm3/Nm between room temperature and 800 °C. Such remarkable wear resistance heretofore represents one of the highest wear resistance reported for the bulk alloys or composites, and originates from the multi-type adaptive friction interface protection governed by intrinsically nano-coupled grains and nanoprecipitates. This cooperative heterostructure releases gradient frictional stress in stages upon wear at room temperature through the coexistence of multiple deformation pathways while activating a dense nanocrystalline glaze layer upon wear at 800 °C to minimize adhesive and oxidative wear. Evidence of Inverse Hall-Petch Behavior and Low Friction and Wear in High Entropy Alloys

Abstract: AbstractWe present evidence of inverse Hall-Petch behavior for a single-phase high entropy alloy (CoCrFeMnNi) in ultra-high vacuum and show that it is associated with low friction coefficients (~0.3). Grain size measurements by STEM validate a recently proposed dynamic amorphization model that accurately predicts grain size-dependent shear strength in the inverse Hall-Petch regime. Wear rates in the initially soft (coarse grained) material were shown to be remarkably low (~10–6 mm3/N-m), the lowest for any HEA tested in an inert environment where oxidation and the formation of mixed metal-oxide films is mitigated. The combined high wear resistance and low friction are linked to the formation of an ultra-nanocrystalline near-surface layer. The dynamic amorphization model was also used to predict an average high angle grain boundary energy (0.87 J/m2). This value was used to explain cavitation-induced nanoporosity found in the highly deformed surface layer, a phenomenon that has been linked to superplasticity.Subject terms: Structural materials, Structural properties

WC-High Entropy Alloy Reinforced Long Life Self-Grinding Silage Knife Prepared by Laser Cladding

Abstract: AbstractThe working environment of agricultural knives is bad, which makes the knives wear out easily. A wear resistant layer of AlCoCrFeNi high entropy alloy (HEA) reinforced by tungsten carbide (WC) was prepared by laser cladding on one side of the cutting edge of a 65 Mn silage knife. Both the effects of WC addition on the microstructure and mechanical properties of AlCoCrFeNi (WC)x (x = 0, 0.1, 0.2 and 0.3 in mass percentage) alloys were investigated. All experimental alloys displayed a crystalline structure of simple body centered cubic (BCC). The hardness of the cladding layer increases with the increase of WC content, and the hardness value enhances from 740 HV0.2 to 1060 HV0.2. A self-grinding edge was formed during working for the cladded knives. The cutting quality can be improved and the service life of agricultural knives can be increased meanwhile. The weight loss rate of untreated knives was about 2.64 times that of the cladded knives after a 76 h field experiment.Keywords: high entropy alloy, WC particles, self-grinding, microstructure, wear resistance
